$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F})+\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}_{P}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F})+\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}_{P}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{P},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F})+\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}_{P}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{P},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle k\cdot(n_{r-1}-1)\cdot f_{r}\cdot(t-1), $$

since there are $f_{r}$ fooling blocks of $n_{r-1}-1$ fooling vertices each, and every fooling vertex communicates at most $k$ bits in each of the first $t-1$ rounds. Going back to the expectation, we finally get

$$ \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\frac{1}{p_{r}}\cdot\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\frac{k\cdot n_{r-1}\cdot f_{r}\cdot r}{p_{r}} \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\epsilon_{r}, $$

by the assumption $r=o(\log k)$ .

#### Proof of the second statement:

The proof is quite similar to the first one. Our goal is still to the bound the following summation:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}), $$

as ${\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}=({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F})$ and by the chain rule of mutual information (Fact A.1-(6)). Again we bound the first term above as follows.

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{<i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) {\mathsf{G}}_{i}\perp{\mathsf{G}}_{<i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}} \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}_{P},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F})+\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}_{P},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F})+\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F})+\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}_{P}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}). $$

Plugging into Equation 17, we have

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F})+\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F})+\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}_{P}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F})+\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F})+\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}_{P}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{P},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F})+\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F})+\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}_{P}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{P},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}). \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F})+\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F}) \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle k\cdot(n_{r-1}-1)\cdot f_{r}\cdot t, $$

by counting the total communication of all fooling vertices. The desired upper bound on the expectation is derived similarly to the first statement.

Technically, it is actually possible to prove the following similar to Claim 5.6:

$$ \mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P}\,;{\mathsf{G}}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\leq\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}), $$

which would justify the intuition we provided for Claim 5.6 even better. However, the proof of Lemma 5.5 is complicated by the fact that neither ${\mathsf{G}}_{i}\perp{\mathsf{G}}_{<i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)}_{P},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}$ nor ${\mathsf{G}}_{i}\perp{\mathsf{G}}_{<i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq t)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}$ is true. In general ${\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P}$ depends on ${\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)}_{F}$ , which in turn is able to correlate ${\mathsf{G}}_{i}$ and ${\mathsf{G}}_{-i}$ . At the core of the proof of Lemma 5.5 is applying the chain rule of mutual information (Fact A.1-(6)) over all ${\mathsf{G}}_{i}$ . To have the chain rule go through in the correct direction, what we need is the conditional independence between all ${\mathsf{G}}_{i}$ . As a result, we are forced to rewrite the summation as in Equations 16 and 17 such that the conditional independence between all ${\mathsf{G}}_{i}$ hold, and then conduct a more careful analysis to bound the amount of correlation caused by the messages of fooling vertices. The current form of Claim 5.6 turns out to be more appropriate for this purpose.

Combining Lemmas 5.3, 5.4 and 5.5, the following corollary follows directly from Pinsker’s inequality (Fact A.8). It essentially captures our initial intuition that the final blackboard ${\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)}$ sampled by $\tau_{i}$ is close to the true distribution on average over all possible $i\in[p_{r}]$ .

#### Corollary 5.7.

Let $\mu$ be the true distribution for $({\mathsf{G}},{\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})$ in $\pi$ and for $i\in[p_{r}]$ , $\mu_{i}$ be the marginal distribution of $\mu$ for $({\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})$ . For $i\in[p_{r}]$ , let $\nu_{i}$ be the distribution of $({\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})$ defined by

$$ \displaystyle\nu_{i}({\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle:=\mu({\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\cdot\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\cdot\prod_{u\in{\mathsf{\Sigma}}({\mathscr{P}}_{i})}\mu({\mathsf{T}}_{i}(u)\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i}(u),{\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\qquad\cdot\prod_{t\in[r]}\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\cdot\prod_{t\in[r]}\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}) \displaystyle\qquad\cdot\prod_{t\in[2,r]}\prod_{u\in{\mathsf{\Sigma}}({\mathscr{P}}_{i})}\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i}(u)\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{i}(u),{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}). $$

It holds that

$$ \Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}\leq\frac{1}{k\cdot n_{r-1}}. $$

#### Proof.

Firstly, we convert the statements of Lemmas 5.3 and 5.5 to the language of total variation distance. For each $i\in[p_{r}]$ , we have

$$ \displaystyle\Exp_{({\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{({\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\|\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\Exp_{({\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\sqrt{\mathbb{D}(\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})~||~\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}))} \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\sqrt{\Exp_{({\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\mathbb{D}(\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})~||~\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}}))} \sqrt{\cdot} \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\sqrt{\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i}\,;{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{\Sigma}})} \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\epsilon_{r}^{1/2}. $$

Meanwhile, for each $t\in[r]$ , we can get

$$ \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\|\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\sqrt{\mathbb{D}(\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})~||~\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}))} \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\sqrt{\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\mathbb{D}(\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})~||~\mu({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}))} \sqrt{\cdot} \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\sqrt{\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,-i}\,;{\mathsf{G}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})} \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\epsilon_{r}^{1/2}, $$

and similarly

$$ \Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F}\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{F}\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}\leq\epsilon_{r}^{1/2}. $$

We also trivially have

$$ \Exp_{({\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{T}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{T}}_{i}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(1)}_{P,i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}=0, $$

by Lemma 5.4 for each $i\in[p_{r}]$ , and

$$ \Exp_{({\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(t)}_{P,i}\mid{\mathsf{G}}_{i},{\mathsf{M}}^{(<t)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}=0, $$

by the second statement of Remark 5.2 for each $t\in[2,r]$ . Additionally observe that

$$ \Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}=0, $$

since ${\mathsf{\Sigma}}$ is a uniformly random permutation drawn independent of ${\mathsf{B}}_{i}$ . Combining all these conditional distributions using the chain rule of total variation distance (Fact A.6), it holds that

$$ \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{T}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{T}}_{i},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\epsilon_{r}^{1/2}\cdot(2r+1) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\frac{(2r+1)}{k^{2}\cdot n_{r-1}} \displaystyle\leq{} \displaystyle\frac{1}{k\cdot n_{r-1}}, $$

by the linearity of expectation and the assumption $r=o(\log k)$ . This concludes the proof as marginalization can never increase total variation distance (Fact A.7).

In Corollary 5.7, note that $\mu$ and $\mu_{i}$ are the true distributions in $\pi$ while $\nu_{i}$ is the distribution sampled by $\tau_{i}$ . We conclude this section by finishing the proof of Lemma 5.1.

#### Proof of Lemma 5.1.

For each $i\in[p_{r}]$ , define ${\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}_{i}\in\left\{0,1\right\}$ to be $1$ if and only if the referee of $\pi$ outputs a valid maximal independent set $\Gamma$ for an $r$ -round instance such that $\Gamma\cap{\mathsf{\Sigma}}({\mathscr{P}}_{i})$ is also a valid maximal independent set for the induced subgraph on ${\mathsf{\Sigma}}({\mathscr{P}}_{i})$ . Also define ${\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}\in\left\{0,1\right\}$ to be $1$ if and only if the referee of $\tau_{i}$ outputs a valid maximal independent set for an $(r-1)$ -round instance. Recall that the referee of $\pi$ is a deterministic function of ${\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)}$ , so for each $i\in[p_{r}]$ , the referee of $\tau_{i}$ is a deterministic function of ${\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)}$ and ${\mathsf{\Sigma}}$ , by Algorithm 1.

Firstly imagine the idealized situation where $\tau_{i}$ were able to sample ${\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i}$ precisely following $\mu_{i}$ . Since the marginal distribution for each principal instance in ${\mathcal{D}^{(r)}_{\mathsf{MIS}}}$ is the same as ${\mathcal{D}^{(r-1)}_{\mathsf{MIS}}}$ , by the linearity of expectation we get

$$ \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\Prob_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\mu_{i}}\left({\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}=1\right) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu}\Prob_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\mu}\left({\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}=1\right) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Prob_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{G}},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\left({\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}_{i}=1\right) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\Prob_{i\in[p_{r}]}\left({\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}_{i}=1\right) \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\delta/2, $$

because $\pi$ succeeds with probability $\delta$ by assumption, and conditioned on this event, at least half of the principal instances are solved by Claim 4.3. Now consider the real success probability of $\tau_{i}$ over $\nu_{i}$ . By Fact A.5, we have for each $i\in[p_{r}]$ ,

$$ \displaystyle\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\nu_{i}}\Prob_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\nu_{i}}\left({\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}=1\right) \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\Prob_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\nu_{i}}\left({\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}=1\right) \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\Prob_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\mu_{i}}\left({\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}=1\right)-\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}. $$

Combining Corollary 5.7 with Equations 18 and 19, we finally get

$$ \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\nu_{i}}\Prob_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\nu_{i}}\left({\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}=1\right) \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\Prob_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\mu_{i}}\left({\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}=1\right)-\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\delta/2-1/n_{r-1}, $$

as desired. Picking the index $i^{*}\in[p_{r}]$ that maximizes the success probability of $\tau_{i^{*}}$ concludes the proof.

### 6 The Lower Bound for Approximate Bipartite Matching

In this section we adapt the techniques for maximal independent set to prove the following formal version of Result 2.

#### Theorem 3 (Result 2, formal).

For $r\geq 0$ and any $r$ -round multi-party protocol (deterministic or randomized) in the shared blackboard model for computing a maximal matching or any constant factor approximation to maximum matching on $n$ -vertex (bipartite) graphs, there must exist some vertex communicating at least $\Omega(n^{1/{20}^{r+1}})$ bits in some round.

Intuitively, Distribution 3 and Algorithm 1 make little use of any property specific to independent sets so most of the lemmas hold for matchings as well. For convenience, we first make minor adjustment to the hard distributions in Section 6.1 to better fit the need of approximation, and then present the lower bound proof for approximate matching for general graphs in Section 6.2. It is worth noticing that our constructed instances may not be bipartite in general. Fortunately, Section 6.3 gives a simple reduction to the bipartite case, concluding the proof of Theorem 3.

#### 6.1 A Hard Distribution for Approximate Matching

We use the following base case for approximate matching. The idea is to have maximum matchings of a fixed size that remain hard to approximate. This will help simplify the calculation in later proofs a lot.

#### Distribution 4.

It is easy to see any graph $G$ drawn from ${\mathcal{D}^{(0)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ always has a maximum matching of size $1$ . Recall that protocols for approximate matching are required to output a valid matching (though potentially containing non-existing edges), which is of size at most $k$ . Since the chosen edge $(u,v)$ is sampled uniformly at random from $k^{2}$ possibilities, no protocols can achieve an approximation ratio better than $k^{2}/k=k$ if no information is revealed by the vertices. This is summarized in the following lemma.

#### Lemma 6.1 (Base Case).

Any $0$ -round protocol for computing an approximate matching has an approximation ratio no better than $k$ over ${\mathcal{D}^{(0)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ .

The construction for $r$ -round hard distributions ${\mathcal{D}^{(r)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ is almost the same as for ${\mathcal{D}^{(r)}_{\mathsf{MIS}}}$ . In fact, it can be even simplified in the sense that the “half instances” are sufficient for the purpose of constructing a hard distribution. Concretely, we construct ${\mathcal{D}^{(r)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ recursively as follows.

#### Distribution 5.

It is not hard to verify that $n_{r}\leq k^{{20}^{r+1}}$ still holds for $r\geq 0$ . At a high level, the number of fooling vertices is rather small as $f_{r}\ll p_{r}$ , so their contribution to the size of maximum matchings is limited. On the other hand, a vast majority of matching edges should come from within the principal blocks so a good approximation ratio for $r$ -round instances implies good approximation ratios over all principal $(r-1)$ -round instances on average. Claim 6.2 provides a useful lower bound on the size of maximum matchings for graphs drawn from ${\mathcal{D}^{(r)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ . It will be used in the proof at the very end of this section.

#### Claim 6.2.

Let $\Gamma$ be any valid maximum matching for a graph $G$ drawn from ${\mathcal{D}^{(r)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ . Then,

$$ \displaystyle|\Gamma|\geq\frac{n_{r}}{2k}\cdot\left(1-\sum_{t\in[r]}\frac{f_{t}}{p_{t}}\right)\geq\frac{n_{r}}{4k}. $$

#### Proof.

The base case of $r=0$ holds trivially. For $r\geq 1$ , we know by induction that any principal $(r-1)$ -round instance has a maximum matching of size at least $\frac{n_{r-1}}{2k}\cdot(1-\sum_{t\in[r-1]}f_{t}/p_{t})$ . Since all $p_{r}$ principal blocks are disjoint by our construction in Distribution 5, we get

$$ \displaystyle|\Gamma| \displaystyle\geq p_{r}\cdot\frac{n_{r-1}}{2k}\cdot\left(1-\sum_{t\in[r-1]}\frac{f_{t}}{p_{t}}\right) \displaystyle\geq\frac{p_{r}}{f_{r}+p_{r}}\cdot\frac{n_{r}}{2k}\cdot\left(1-\sum_{t\in[r-1]}\frac{f_{t}}{p_{t}}\right) n_{r}\leq n_{r-1}\cdot(f_{r}+p_{r}) \displaystyle\geq\left(1-\frac{f_{r}}{p_{r}}\right)\cdot\frac{n_{r}}{2k}\cdot\left(1-\sum_{t\in[r-1]}\frac{f_{t}}{p_{t}}\right) \displaystyle\geq\frac{n_{r}}{2k}\cdot\left(1-\sum_{t\in[r]}\frac{f_{t}}{p_{t}}\right). $$

The last inequality of Equation 20 follows from the simple fact that

$$ \sum_{t\in[r]}\frac{f_{t}}{p_{t}}=\sum_{t\in[r]}\frac{1}{k^{6}\cdot n_{t-1}^{3}}\leq\frac{1}{2}, $$

since $r=o(\log k)$ by assumption. This concludes the proof.

#### 6.2 Proof of the Lower Bound for Approximate Matching

The version of Theorem 3 for general graphs is a straightforward corollary of the following distributional lower bound by Yao’s minimax principal [Yao77]. We point out that since any maximal matching is also a $2$ -approximate matching, it is sufficient to prove the hardness of approximate matching.

#### Theorem 4.

For $r=o(\log k)$ , any $r$ -round protocol for computing an approximate matching for general graphs that communicates at most $k$ bits per vertex in every round has an approximation ratio no better than $\Omega(k)$ over ${\mathcal{D}^{(r)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ .

The proof of Theorem 4 is again via a round elimination lemma as shown in Lemma 6.3.

#### Lemma 6.3 (Round Elimination).

For $r=o(\log k)$ and $\alpha=\omega(1/n_{r-1})$ , if there exists an $r$ -round protocol for computing an approximate matching that communicates at most $k$ bits per vertex in every round and has an approximation ratio of $\alpha^{-1}$ over ${\mathcal{D}^{(r)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ , then there also exists an $(r-1)$ -round protocol for computing an approximate matching that communicates at most $k$ bits per vertex in every round and has an approximation ratio of $(\alpha-C/n_{r-1})^{-1}$ over ${\mathcal{D}^{(r-1)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ , for some universal constant $C>0$ .

Before proving Lemma 6.3, which is the main part of this section, we first show it easily implies Theorem 4.

#### Proof of Theorem 4.

Suppose for the purpose of contradiction that there exists an $r$ -round protocol that communicates at most $k$ bits per vertex and that has an approximation ratio of $\alpha^{-1}=o(k)$ over ${\mathcal{D}^{(r)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ . Applying Lemma 6.3 for $r$ times, we obtain a $0$ -round protocol having an approximation ratio of

$$ \left(\alpha-C\cdot\sum_{t\in[r]}\frac{1}{n_{t-1}}\right)^{-1}\leq\left(\alpha-\frac{2C}{n_{0}}\right)^{-1}=o(k), $$

over ${\mathcal{D}^{(0)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ , as $n_{t-1}$ is doubly exponentially increasing, and $\alpha=\omega(1/k),n_{0}=2k$ . However, the existence of such a $0$ -round protocol contradicts the lower bound of Lemma 6.1, concluding the proof.

To prove Lemma 6.3, we use the same approach for simulation as in Algorithm 1. Fix a deterministic $r$ -round protocol $\pi$ on $n_{r}$ vertices that communicates at most $k$ bits per vertex in every round and has an approximation ratio of $\alpha^{-1}$ over ${\mathcal{D}^{(r)}_{\mathsf{MM}}}$ . We define exactly the same set of random variables as in Section 5 and construct the $(r-1)$ -round (randomized) protocols $\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{p_{r}}$ on $n_{r-1}$ vertices, which are identical to Algorithm 1 except for the processing of the final output. Specifically, let $\Gamma$ be the output of the referee of $\pi$ when given ${\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)}$ . The referee of $\tau_{i}$ finally outputs $\Gamma\cap\left({\mathsf{\Sigma}}({\mathscr{P}}_{i})\times{\mathsf{\Sigma}}({\mathscr{P}}_{i})\right)$ , namely the edges within ${\mathsf{\Sigma}}({\mathscr{P}}_{i})$ , for computing approximate matchings. See Algorithm 2 for a recap of the complete simulation protocol for round elimination.

#### Algorithm 2.

It is not hard to verify that Lemmas 5.3, 5.4 and 5.5 and Corollary 5.7 also hold for approximate matching. In fact, each of them follows verbatim as the proofs work in a black-box way. Using all these results, we conclude this section with the proof of Lemma 6.3.

#### Proof of Lemma 6.3.

For any $r$ -round instance, let ${\mathsf{O}}$ be the size of its maximum matching and for each $i\in[p_{r}]$ , ${\mathsf{O}}_{i}$ be the size of the maximum matching for the induced subgraph on ${\mathsf{\Sigma}}({\mathscr{P}}_{i})$ . It always holds that

$$ \displaystyle{\mathsf{O}}\geq\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}{\mathsf{O}}_{i}, $$

since the union of maximum matchings for all principal $(r-1)$ -round instances is always a valid matching for the $r$ -round instance. Define ${\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}$ to be the number of valid edges in $\Gamma\cap E$ , where $E$ is the set of input edges of the $r$ -round instance, and for each $i\in[p_{r}]$ , ${\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}_{i}$ to be the number of valid edges in $\Gamma\cap E\cap\left({\mathsf{\Sigma}}({\mathscr{P}}_{i})\times{\mathsf{\Sigma}}({\mathscr{P}}_{i})\right)$ . It holds that

$$ \displaystyle{\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}\leq n_{r-1}\cdot f_{r}+\sum_{i\in[p_{r}]}{\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}_{i}, $$

because of the fact that the number of disjoint edges incident to fooling vertices is bounded by the total number of fooling vertices. (Recall that the output $\Gamma$ of the referee of $\pi$ must be a set of disjoint edges.) Also define ${\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}$ to be the number of valid edges (i.e. excluding non-existing edges) output by the referee of $\tau_{i}$ for an $(r-1)$ -round instance. Note that the referee of $\pi$ is a deterministic function of ${\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)}$ by assumption, so for each $i\in[p_{r}]$ , the referee of $\tau_{i}$ is a deterministic function of ${\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)}$ and ${\mathsf{\Sigma}}$ , by Algorithm 2.

Again imagine the idealized situation where $\tau_{i}$ were able to sample ${\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i}$ precisely following $\mu_{i}$ . By the linearity of expectation, we have

$$ \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\Exp_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\mu_{i}}\left[{\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}\right] \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu}\Exp_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\mu}\left[{\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}\right] \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{G}},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\left[{\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}_{i}\right] \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\left[{\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}_{i}\right] \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\left[\frac{{\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}-n_{r-1}\cdot f_{r}}{p_{r}}\right] \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\left[\frac{{\mathsf{O}}^{\pi}}{p_{r}}\right]-\frac{n_{r-1}\cdot f_{r}}{p_{r}} \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\alpha\cdot\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\left[\frac{{\mathsf{O}}}{p_{r}}\right]-\frac{n_{r-1}\cdot f_{r}}{p_{r}} \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\alpha\cdot\Exp_{({\mathsf{G}},{\mathsf{\Sigma}})\sim\mu}\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\left[{\mathsf{O}}_{i}\right]-\frac{n_{r-1}\cdot f_{r}}{p_{r}} \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\alpha\cdot\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\nu_{i}}\left[{\mathsf{O}}_{i}\right]-\frac{n_{r-1}\cdot f_{r}}{p_{r}}, $$

as $\mu({\mathsf{B}}_{i})=\nu_{i}({\mathsf{B}}_{i})$ . Meanwhile, for each $i\in[p_{r}]$ , Fact A.5 bounds the real expected matching size of $\tau_{i}$ over $\nu_{i}$ as

$$ \displaystyle\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\nu_{i}}\Exp_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\nu_{i}}\left[{\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}\right] \displaystyle={} \displaystyle\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\Exp_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\nu_{i}}\left[{\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}\right] \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\Exp_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\mu_{i}}\left[{\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}\right]-\frac{n_{r-1}}{2}\cdot\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}, $$

since the size of any matching is at most half of the total number of vertices. Combining Corollary 5.7 with Equations 23 and 24, we have

$$ \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\nu_{i}}\Exp_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\nu_{i}}\left[{\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}\right] \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\Exp_{({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\sim\mu_{i}}\left[{\mathsf{O}}^{\tau}_{i}\right]-\frac{n_{r-1}}{2}\cdot\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\mu_{i}}\|\mu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})-\nu_{i}({\mathsf{M}}^{(\leq r)},{\mathsf{\Sigma}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}_{i})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}} \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\alpha\cdot\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\nu_{i}}\left[{\mathsf{O}}_{i}\right]-\frac{n_{r-1}\cdot f_{r}}{p_{r}}-\frac{n_{r-1}}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{k\cdot n_{r-1}} \displaystyle\geq{} \displaystyle\left(\alpha-\frac{n_{r-1}\cdot f_{r}}{p_{r}\cdot n_{r-1}/(4k)}-\frac{1/(2k)}{n_{r-1}/(4k)}\right)\cdot\Exp_{i\in[p_{r}]}\Exp_{{\mathsf{B}}_{i}\sim\nu_{i}}\left[{\mathsf{O}}_{i}\right], $$

$$ \left(\alpha-\frac{n_{r-1}\cdot f_{r}}{p_{r}\cdot n_{r-1}/(4k)}-\frac{1/(2k)}{n_{r-1}/(4k)}\right)^{-1}\leq\left(\alpha-O(\frac{1}{n_{r-1}})\right)^{-1}, $$

as claimed.

#### 6.3 A Reduction to Bipartite Graphs

The following reduction, together with the lower bound for approximate matching for general graphs shown in Section 6.2, concludes the proof of Theorem 3.

#### Lemma 6.4.

For $r,\alpha\geq 1$ , if there exists an $r$ -round protocol for computing an $\alpha$ -approximate bipartite matching for bipartite graphs, then there also exists an $r$ -round protocol for computing a $2\alpha$ -approximate matching for general graphs, with exactly the same bandwidth.

#### Proof.

Let $\pi$ be a protocol for bipartite graphs. We construct a corresponding protocol $\pi^{\prime}$ for general graphs as follows. On a given input graph $G=(V,E)$ with $n$ vertices, the vertices in $\pi^{\prime}$ jointly sample $z\in\left\{0,1\right\}^{n}$ uniformly at random using public randomness. Let $L=\left\{v\in V\mid z_{v}=0\right\}$ and $R=\left\{v\in V\mid z_{v}=1\right\}$ . Note that all vertices agree on $L,R$ since they can be easily computed from $z$ . Also let $G^{\prime}=(V,E^{\prime})$ be the bipartite subgraph of $G$ where only edges across the cut $(L,R)$ are preserved, i.e. $E^{\prime}=\left\{(u,v)\in E\mid z_{u}\neq z_{v}\right\}$ . Then all vertices run $\pi$ on $G^{\prime}$ as if the neighbors of a vertex $v\in V$ are $N_{G^{\prime}}(v)=\left\{u\in N_{G}(v)\mid z_{u}\neq z_{v}\right\}$ . The referee of $\pi^{\prime}$ simply outputs the answer given by the referee of $\pi$ .

It is easy to see $\pi^{\prime}$ has the same number of rounds and exactly the same bandwidth as $\pi$ . Moreover, observe that $G^{\prime}$ is essentially a random bipartition of $G$ so half of the original edges are dropped in expectation. In particular, we have $\Exp_{z}[\mu(G^{\prime})]\geq\mu(G)/2$ . (Recall that $\mu(\cdot)$ denotes the size of the maximum matching.) Therefore, an $\alpha$ -approximate bipartite matching for $G^{\prime}$ (over the randomness of $z$ ) is also a $2\alpha$ -approximate matching for $G$ by definition.

## Appendix

### Appendix A Basic Tools From Information Theory

We now briefly introduce some definitions from information theory that are needed in this paper. For a random variable ${\mathsf{A}}$ , we use $\textnormal{\text{supp}}({\mathsf{A}})$ to denote the support of ${\mathsf{A}}$ and $\textnormal{dist}({\mathsf{A}})$ to denote its distribution. When it is clear from context, we may abuse the notation and use ${\mathsf{A}}$ directly instead of $\textnormal{dist}({\mathsf{A}})$ , for example, write $A\sim{\mathsf{A}}$ to mean $A\sim\textnormal{dist}({\mathsf{A}})$ , i.e., $A$ is sampled from the distribution of random variable ${\mathsf{A}}$ .

We denote the Shannon entropy of a random variable ${\mathsf{A}}$ by $\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}})$ , which is defined as:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}})=\sum_{A\in\textnormal{\text{supp}}({\mathsf{A}})}\Prob\left({\mathsf{A}}=A\right)\cdot\log\frac{1}{\Prob\left({\mathsf{A}}=A\right)}. $$

The conditional entropy of ${\mathsf{A}}$ conditioned on ${\mathsf{B}}$ is denoted by $\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}})$ and defined as:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}})=\Exp_{B\sim{\mathsf{B}}}\left[\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}=B)\right], $$

where $\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}=B)$ is defined in a standard way by using the distribution of ${\mathsf{A}}$ conditioned on the event ${\mathsf{B}}=B$ in the previous equation. The mutual information of two random variables ${\mathsf{A}}$ and ${\mathsf{B}}$ is denoted by $\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}})$ and defined as:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}})=\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}})-\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}})=\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{B}})-\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{A}}). $$

The conditional mutual information $\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})$ is $\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})-\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}})$ and hence by linearity of expectation:

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})=\Exp_{C\sim{\mathsf{C}}}\left[\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}}=C)\right]. $$

We also use the following standard measures of distance (or divergence) between distributions.

#### KL-divergence.

For two distributions $\mu$ and $\nu$ , the Kullback-Leibler divergence between $\mu$ and $\nu$ is denoted by $\mathbb{D}(\mu~||~\nu)$ and defined as:

$$ \mathbb{D}(\mu~||~\nu)=\Exp_{a\sim\mu}\Big[\log\frac{\mu(a)}{\nu(a)}\Big]. $$

#### Total variation distance.

We denote the total variation distance between two distributions $\mu$ and $\nu$ on the same support $\Omega$ by $\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}$ , defined as:

$$ \|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}=\max_{\Omega^{\prime}\subseteq\Omega}\left(\mu(\Omega^{\prime})-\nu(\Omega^{\prime})\right)=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\sum_{x\in\Omega}\left|{\mu(x)-\nu(x)}\right|. $$

We refer the interested readers to the textbook by Cover and Thomas [CT06] for an excellent introduction to the field of information theory.

#### A.1 Useful Properties of Entropy and Mutual Information

We use the following basic properties of entropy and mutual information throughout.

#### Fact A.1 (cf. [CT06]).

Let ${\mathsf{A}}$ , ${\mathsf{B}}$ , ${\mathsf{C}}$ , and ${\mathsf{D}}$ be four (possibly correlated) random variables.

- 1. $0\leq\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}})\leq\log{\left|{\textnormal{\text{supp}}({\mathsf{A}})}\right|}$ . The right equality holds iff $\textnormal{dist}({\mathsf{A}})$ is uniform.

- 2. $\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})\geq 0$ . The equality holds iff ${\mathsf{A}}$ and ${\mathsf{B}}$ are independent conditioned on ${\mathsf{C}}$ .

- 3. Conditioning on a random variable reduces entropy: $\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}})\leq\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}})$ . The equality holds iff ${\mathsf{A}}\perp{\mathsf{C}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}$ .

- 4. Subadditivity of entropy: $\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}},{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})\leq\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid C)+\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})$ .

- 5. Chain rule for entropy: $\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}},{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})=\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})+\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{A}})$ .

- 6. Chain rule for mutual information: $\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}},{\mathsf{B}}\,;{\mathsf{C}}\mid{\mathsf{D}})=\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{C}}\mid{\mathsf{D}})+\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{B}}\,;{\mathsf{C}}\mid{\mathsf{A}},{\mathsf{D}})$ .

- 7. Data processing inequality: for a deterministic function $f({\mathsf{A}})$ , $\mathbb{I}(f({\mathsf{A}})\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})\leq\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})$ .

We also use the following propositions, regarding the effect of conditioning on mutual information.

#### Proposition A.2.

For random variables ${\mathsf{A}},{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}}$ , if ${\mathsf{A}}\perp{\mathsf{D}}\mid{\mathsf{C}}$ , then,

$$ \mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})\leq\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}}). $$

#### Proof.

Since ${\mathsf{A}}$ and ${\mathsf{D}}$ are independent conditioned on ${\mathsf{C}}$ , by Fact A.1-(3), $\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})=\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}})$ and $\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{B}})\geq\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{D}})$ . We have,

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})-\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{B}})=\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}})-\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{B}}) \displaystyle\leq\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}})-\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{D}})=\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}}).\penalty\hskip 0.0pt\hskip 15.00002pt\penalty\vrule height=7.5pt,width=5.0pt,depth=2.5pt $$

#### Proposition A.3.

For random variables ${\mathsf{A}},{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}}$ , if ${\mathsf{A}}\perp{\mathsf{D}}\mid{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}}$ , then,

$$ \mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})\geq\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}}). $$

#### Proof.

Since ${\mathsf{A}}\perp{\mathsf{D}}\mid{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}}$ , by Fact A.1-(3), $\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}})=\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}})$ . Moreover, since conditioning can only reduce the entropy (again by Fact A.1-(3)),

$$ \displaystyle\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})-\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}})\geq\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{D}},{\mathsf{C}})-\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}}) \displaystyle=\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{D}},{\mathsf{C}})-\mathbb{H}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}})=\mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}},{\mathsf{D}}).\penalty\hskip 0.0pt\hskip 15.00002pt\penalty\vrule height=7.5pt,width=5.0pt,depth=2.5pt $$

#### A.2 Measures of Distance Between Distributions

The following states the relation between mutual information and KL-divergence.

#### Fact A.4.

For random variables ${\mathsf{A}},{\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}}$ ,

$$ \mathbb{I}({\mathsf{A}}\,;{\mathsf{B}}\mid{\mathsf{C}})=\Exp_{(b,c)\sim{({\mathsf{B}},{\mathsf{C}})}}\Big[\mathbb{D}(\textnormal{dist}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{B}}=b,{\mathsf{C}}=c)~||~\textnormal{dist}({\mathsf{A}}\mid{\mathsf{C}}=c))\Big]. $$

We use the following basic properties of total variation distance.

#### Fact A.5.

Suppose $\mu$ and $\nu$ are two distributions for a random variable ${\mathsf{X}}$ , then,

$$ \Exp_{\mu}\left[{\mathsf{X}}\right]\leq\Exp_{\nu}\left[{\mathsf{X}}\right]+\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}\cdot\max_{X_{0}\in\textnormal{\text{supp}}({\mathsf{X}})}X_{0}. $$

#### Fact A.6.

Suppose $\mu$ and $\nu$ are two distributions for the tuple $({\mathsf{X}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathsf{X}}_{t})$ , then,

$$ \|\mu({\mathsf{X}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathsf{X}}_{t})-\nu({\mathsf{X}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathsf{X}}_{t})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}\leq\sum_{i=1}^{n}\Exp_{(X_{1},\ldots,X_{i-1})\sim\mu}\|\mu({\mathsf{X}}_{i}\mid X_{1},\ldots,X_{i-1})-\nu({\mathsf{X}}_{i}\mid X_{1},\ldots,X_{i-1})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}. $$

#### Fact A.7.

Suppose $\mu$ and $\nu$ are two distributions for the pair $({\mathsf{X}},{\mathsf{Y}})$ , then,

$$ \|\mu({\mathsf{X}})-\nu({\mathsf{X}})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}\leq\|\mu({\mathsf{X}},{\mathsf{Y}})-\nu({\mathsf{X}},{\mathsf{Y}})\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}. $$

The following Pinsker’s inequality bounds the total variation distance between two distributions based on their KL-divergence.

#### Fact A.8 (Pinsker’s inequality).

For any distributions $\mu$ and $\nu$ , $\|\mu-\nu\|_{\mathrm{tvd}}\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\cdot\mathbb{D}(\mu~||~\nu)}.$
